page: The Vultr voc-s-4c-32gb-960s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance equipped with 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 2 physical AMD EPYC cores running at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The platform features 32.0 GB of system memory, providing a ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU that positions the instance for memory-intensive deployments. Storage is bundled directly as a 960 GB local NVMe SSD, and network connectivity includes 1 complimentary public IPv4 address without discrete GPU acceleration.

Hardware capabilities incorporate AVX-512 instruction extensions including VNNI and BF16, alongside cryptographic accelerators like AES and SHA-NI. In benchmark evaluations, the processor exhibits top-tier single-core compute performance in stress-ng at 3,432.18, alongside strong single-threaded throughput in gzip compression at 32.27 GB/s. Memory performance is solid, evidenced by large-block uncached write bandwidth of 122.3 GB/s and a strong PassMark memory benchmark score of 2,805.81. In contrast, multi-core metrics reflect the physical dual-core footprint, delivering average tier scores in Geekbench multi-core and PassMark CPU suites.

Workload tradeoffs emerge under highly concurrent or web-oriented tasks. Static web serving throughput reaches 3.86 GB/s and PassMark database operations show lower relative efficiency, while multi-threaded bzip3 decompression scales moderately. The lack of hardware accelerators limits large language model inference to lightweight models. However, the generous memory capacity combined with dedicated single-thread execution and high local NVMe storage density delivers reliable qualitative cost efficiency for in-memory key-value caching such as Redis, text processing, intermediate compilation jobs, and persistent backend services.

The CPU architecture integrates AVX-512, VNNI, and cryptographic hardware extensions. Benchmark data reveals top-tier single-core compute performance and strong large-block memory write bandwidth reaching 122.3 GB/s, alongside strong single-threaded compression speeds. However, multi-threaded throughput and static web transfer rates show moderate-to-low efficiency, reflecting physical dual-core limitations under high parallel load.
